db_evidence.notes: Both official clue windows are textually retrievable in episodes (186857-186917: 'jokes the fan is the first messy fan... the two laugh'; 263511-263541: 'excitedly chants about ronaldo and messi, declares messi the better player') but neither episode's auto-generated caption text reads as displeasure - both read as joking/excited banter. This means text-only retrieval (semantic_search/run_sql over episode captions) systematically under-surfaces the two official clue intervals for a 'displeasure' query, and correctly identifying them requires clip_qa visual verification of tone/body-language that the captions do not carry - and even clip_qa's answer flips between 'not displeased' and 'displeased' for the identical 186857-186917 window depending on how leadingly the question is phrased (rollout 0 neutral -> No; rollout 2 leading -> Yes).

root_causes: The LLM judge scores purely by matching the candidate's final stated count against the reference text 'Twice' (question+reference+candidate only, no evidence/trace access) - it does not check whether the cited timestamps/episodes are the correct ones, so three rollouts scored 5 despite citing three largely non-overlapping pairs of 'displeasure' instances, at least one of which (rollout 1's 276,921-276,951 'criticizes messi's world cup performance') is a criticism of Messi-the-player rather than displeasure at a fan's shirt.

Episode/topic_fact captions describing the two officially-tagged clue moments (186857-186917 and 263511-263541) read as joking/excited banter, not displeasure, so text-only retrieval (semantic_search, run_sql keyword scans for 'angry'/'upset'/'displeased') tends to miss or deprioritize them; visual (clip_qa) inspection is required to correctly read tone.

clip_qa answers are highly sensitive to question framing: a neutral question ('Is he displeased, annoyed, or trying to get the fan away?') on window 186857-186917 returned 'not displeased', while a leading/compound question ('...does he visibly react with displeasure or try to get away from the fan?') on the same window returned 'Yes'. Rollouts that used leading yes/no clip_qa phrasing (rollouts 2, 4) got affirmative answers more readily, which in rollout 4's case cascaded into over-counting to three by confirming displeasure at low-confidence, off-clue windows (290k, 308k) that no other rollout surfaced.

Rollout 0 undercounted because its keyword/semantic searches never surfaced the 263,511-263,541 window at all (it does not contain displeasure-sounding language in the caption), so it only found one confirmed displeasure episode and stopped there.
what_worked: Rollouts 2 and 3 converged independently on the same two-episode structure (Beijing 186857-186917 + Chongqing 239696-239906) and correctly applied the counting-and-ordering skill's guidance to dedup multiple fans/shirts within one continuous crowd scene into a single 'occurrence', landing on the right final count.

Rollout 1 found the true second official clue window (263511-263541) via broad SQL window scans even though its caption text does not read as displeasure - broad window scanning around 'messi' keyword hits across the full 150k-320k range helped surface it despite the text tone mismatch.
transferable_lessons: For emotion/reaction-based counting questions (e.g. 'displeased', 'annoyed'), do not trust episode/topic_fact caption wording alone to decide tone - captions frequently describe joking/laughing surface behavior even when the underlying reaction (per the reference) is meant to register as displeasure; always visually verify candidate windows with clip_qa.

Phrase clip_qa questions neutrally/open-endedly (e.g. 'Describe his reaction; is it displeasure, excitement, both, or neither?') rather than as a leading yes/no question ('does he become displeased...?'), since leading phrasing measurably biases the visual sub-agent toward confirming the premise, which can inflate counts when leading questions are asked across many marginal candidate windows.

When several candidate 'messi + fan' windows exist across a multi-hour timeline, cross-check candidates against each other for consistency (e.g. do other tool calls or other rollouts also surface this window?) before including a low-confidence clip_qa 'yes' in a final count - rollout 4's over-count came from accepting several one-off leading-question confirmations that no other independent evidence path corroborated.

Broaden SQL/semantic search beyond exact emotion keywords ('angry','displeased','upset') when hunting for a reaction event, since the reference reaction may be captioned in neutral or even celebratory language by the automated captioner; scan all 'messi'-keyword hits across the full time range and visually re-verify each, rather than filtering by emotion words at the retrieval stage.
open_questions: What is the ground-truth intended pair of 'displeasure' moments corresponding to the two official clue_interval windows (186857-186917 and 263511-263541)? Their episode captions read as joking/excited, and clip_qa reads differ depending on question framing (No vs Yes for the same 186857-186917 window), so it's unresolved from available evidence which framing is actually visually correct.

Is the judge intentionally evidence-agnostic (question+reference+candidate only), or is this a training-free harness limitation where trace/evidence access for the judge was simply not wired in? This determines whether the observed lenient/inconsistent-instance scoring behavior is by design.

Is rollout 1's second cited instance (276,921-276,951, 'criticizes messi's world cup performance, calling him undeserving and short') actually a case of displeasure at a *fan wearing a Messi shirt*, or is it Speed criticizing Messi's playing ability unrelated to any fan's shirt? If the latter, rollout 1 arrived at the correct count via an evidentially wrong second instance, which the judge did not detect.
